The Late Triassic sauropodomorph Plateosaurus engelhardti has been the subject of considerable palaeobiological speculation regarding its growth and reproduction. Based on comparative physiology with extant archosaurs and lepidosaurs, its maximum reproductive rate has been tentatively estimated. Under a body temperature regime typical of a large ectothermic or inertial homeothermic reptile of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], females may have produced approximately 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per clutch], with the potential to lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], yielding an annual output of 30 eggs. This value is highly speculative and derived from scaling relationships with body mass. The estimated neonatal wet weight at birth is roughly 1,000 grams [Wwb = roughly 1,000 grams], a figure consistent with the hatchling masses predicted for other large-bodied, non-avian dinosaurs. These hatchlings would have emerged from relatively large, parchment-shelled eggs after an extended incubation period, entering a world of seasonal aridity and competing with insects and early crocodylomorphs for resources.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult of Plateosaurus engelhardti has been estimated at approximately 2,000,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,000,000 grams], placing it among the larger terrestrial herbivores of the Norian stage. This mass, roughly equivalent to 2 metric tons, represents a maximum adult body size that few contemporary herbivores could match. Growth to this size likely required a sustained phase of rapid mass gain during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, facilitated by a high-fibre, plant-based diet of ferns and cycads. Evidence from bone histology suggests that individuals grew in a cyclical pattern, with annuli indicating periodic slowdowns possibly linked to seasonal resource scarcity. Reaching such a massive body size would have conferred significant advantages in terms of predator defence and thermoregulatory inertia, but would also have demanded substantial daily energetic costs for tissue upkeep and locomotion. The attainment of this asymptotic mass likely preceded or coincided with the onset of reproductive activity.

Concerning longevity, the maximum lifespan of Plateosaurus engelhardti in the wild has been projected to be around 20 years [am = around 20 years] at a regulated body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This figure, while speculative, aligns with the estimated lifespans of other large non-avian dinosaurs derived from growth ring counts in fossilized long bones. A two-decade lifespan would have allowed for multiple reproductive seasons, giving each individual ample opportunity to contribute offspring to the next generation. The attainment of such an age would have required surviving the perils of predation, disease, and environmental stochasticity, particularly during the vulnerable hatchling and juvenile phases. Comparative analysis with extant reptiles of similar body mass, such as the larger varanid lizards and crocodilians, supports the plausibility of a 20-year maximum lifespan for a multi-tonne herbivore in a seasonal Triassic environment. Natural mortality would likely have resulted from senescence, injury, or catastrophic events like drought.

The time from birth to the onset of puberty in Plateosaurus engelhardti is similarly speculative but has been estimated at approximately 13 years from birth [tp = approximately 13 years from birth] under a body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This protracted juvenile period is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes extensive somatic growth before the initiation of gametogenesis and first reproduction. Reaching sexual maturation at such a late age would have allowed individuals to attain a substantial body size, thereby reducing the risk of predation and improving the likelihood of successful nesting. This pace of life is reminiscent of that seen in large-bodied extant reptiles such as sea turtles and crocodiles, which also delay reproductive maturity for many years. The onset of gonadal activation at this stage would have marked a significant physiological transition, with resources then being partly directed toward the production of large, yolked eggs each breeding season. It is likely that only individuals who successfully navigated the challenges of the extended juvenile phase would ultimately contribute to the population's genetic legacy.

A comprehensive life table for Plateosaurus engelhardti reveals a slow, K-selected life history. Hatchlings emerged at roughly 1,000 grams [Wwb = roughly 1,000 grams], a very substantial birth mass compared to most reptiles, and would have been relatively precocial, likely capable of foraging soon after eclosion. The period of rapid juvenile growth culminated in the attainment of an adult mass of roughly 2,000,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 2,000,000 grams], a size at which individuals would have been largely immune to predation by contemporary theropods. Sexual maturity was reached at around 13 years after hatching [tp = around 13 years after hatching], a delay that reflects the immense energetic investment required to build a multi-tonne body at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The species' maximum reproductive output, when considered under a constant internal temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], translated to an annual production of about 30 eggs per female per year, a modest fecundity for a reptile of such size. Finally, a potential maximum lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] capped the reproductive window, suggesting that relatively few reproductive events were available to each individual, placing a premium on the survival of each clutch at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C].
